paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Twenty years ago, a beehive on a city rooftop would have struck most people as an eccentric hobby. Today hives can be found on the roofs of offices, hotels, museums and department stores, and beekeeping associations in many large cities report that their membership has more than doubled. The main motive is concern. News of falling bee numbers in the countryside has persuaded thousands of urban residents that they can help by keeping colonies of their own, and companies have been quick to see the public relations value of a hive on the roof and a jar of honey for visiting clients.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: What surprises many newcomers is that bees often seem to do better in cities than in rural areas. Modern farmland frequently consists of huge fields of a single crop that flowers for only a few weeks, after which there is almost nothing for a foraging bee to eat. Chemical sprays add a further risk. A city, by contrast, offers a patchwork of parks, private gardens, street trees, window boxes and neglected corners, with the result that something is in flower from early spring until late autumn. Cities are also warmer than the surrounding countryside because of the "urban heat island" effect, which lengthens the period each year in which bees can leave the hive. In several surveys, urban colonies produced more honey and were more likely to survive the winter than comparable colonies in the country.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Ecologists, however, are uneasy about the way the story has been told. The honey bee, they point out, is a managed animal, kept by people in the way that farmers keep cattle, and as a species it is in no danger of disappearing. The insects that are genuinely in decline are wild bees, a group of several thousand species, most of them solitary, which nest in bare soil, dead wood or hollow stems rather than in hives. Wild bees and honey bees feed on the same flowers. When the number of hives in a city rises sharply, researchers have found, the wild species may be forced to travel further for food or to go without. In one study, wild bees visited noticeably fewer flowers in neighbourhoods where hive numbers were highest.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: This has led to calls for limits. A city can only provide so much nectar and pollen, and scientists who have attempted to measure it suggest that the flowers within a typical city boundary can support no more than a handful of hives per square kilometre before competition begins. A few local authorities have responded by introducing a registration scheme that requires beekeepers to register their hives and to say where they are kept. Supporters of the idea argue that the rule would let planners spot areas that are becoming overcrowded. Critics reply that it is difficult to enforce, since a hive on a roof or in a back garden is easily hidden.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Where the hive is placed also matters, and urban beekeepers have become inventive. Rooftops are popular because the bees fly above the heads of pedestrians and the colonies are safe from thieves and vandals, although the hives can be exposed to strong wind and summer heat. Railway embankments, rarely visited by the public, form long corridors of wild flowers that bees can follow for kilometres. School grounds are valued for a different reason: children who help to inspect a hive learn about insects, food and the seasons at first hand. Cemeteries, finally, combine silence with a rich mixture of flowering trees, shrubs and uncut grass, and are among the most productive sites of all. Private balconies, on the other hand, are generally discouraged, because hives kept so close to neighbours are likely to lead to complaints.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A final question is whether city honey is safe to eat. Many people assume that it must be contaminated by traffic fumes and industrial dust. Laboratory tests on honey from several cities have, however, found levels of heavy metals below the safety limits, probably because nectar is carried directly from flower to hive and is changed by the bees' own bodies before it is stored. What does vary is the taste. Honey from a district lined with lime trees is pale and delicate, while honey from an area of overgrown gardens may be dark and strong, and some producers now sell "single-street" honey to customers who like to know exactly where it came from.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Few experts now argue that urban beekeeping will save the world's bees, and many would say that it was never likely to. Its real benefits are social and educational. It brings people into contact with nature, gives schools and community groups a practical project, and often leads beekeepers to take an interest in the wider environment. The most effective help for pollinators, specialists suggest, is rather simpler: plant a wide variety of flowers, leave part of the garden uncut, and provide places where solitary bees can nest. A number of former beekeepers have taken exactly this advice, trading their hives for a pile of old logs and a few drilled blocks of wood, and have found that the wild visitors arrive on their own.

blocks.instructions: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

questions.q: According to paragraph B, bees often do well in cities because
options: there are fewer species of flower than in the countryside.
colonies are kept in much larger numbers than on farms.
a variety of plants flowers over a longer part of the year.
city bees do not need to travel away from the hive.
questions.explain: Đoạn B: thành phố có công viên, vườn, cây ven đường nên "something is in flower from early spring until late autumn". Các lựa chọn khác không được nhắc đến hoặc ngược với bài.

questions.q: What point does the writer make about honey bees in paragraph C?
options: They are not the type of bee that is most at risk.
They are less well adapted to cities than wild bees.
They nest in the same places as solitary bees.
They are kept in the countryside more than in cities.
questions.explain: Đoạn C: ong mật là loài được nuôi, "in no danger of disappearing"; các loài đang suy giảm là ong hoang dã. Ong hoang dã mới làm tổ trong đất, thân cây rỗng (loại C).

questions.q: Why does the writer mention a registration scheme in paragraph D?
options: To show that beekeeping is becoming a profitable business.
To explain why beekeepers prefer to keep hives in back gardens.
To argue that scientists have measured the supply of nectar accurately.
To give an example of how some authorities are trying to limit hive numbers.
questions.explain: Đoạn D: do có lời kêu gọi giới hạn, một số chính quyền đưa ra chế độ đăng ký tổ ong để phát hiện khu vực quá đông. Đây là ví dụ về việc hạn chế số tổ ong.

questions.q: What is the writer's main view of urban beekeeping in paragraph G?
options: It is a dangerous hobby that should be stopped.
Its main value lies in education and community rather than saving bees.
It is the most effective way of helping pollinators.
It has helped experts to find new species of wild bee.
questions.explain: Đoạn G: lợi ích thực sự của nghề nuôi ong đô thị là "social and educational"; cách giúp thụ phấn hiệu quả hơn là trồng hoa và để chỗ cho ong đơn độc làm tổ.

blocks.instructions: Complete the sentences below. Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage for each answer.

questions.q: Cities lengthen the bees' working year because of the "urban ______" effect.
questions.explain: Đoạn B: "the 'urban heat island' effect, which lengthens the period each year in which bees can leave the hive".

questions.q: Most wild bees are ______ and nest in soil, dead wood or hollow stems.
questions.explain: Đoạn C: ong hoang dã gồm hàng nghìn loài, "most of them solitary", làm tổ trong đất, gỗ mục hoặc thân cây rỗng.

questions.q: Some local authorities now require beekeepers to ______ their hives.
questions.explain: Đoạn D: chế độ đăng ký yêu cầu người nuôi ong "to register their hives and to say where they are kept".

questions.q: Tests found that city honey contained levels of heavy ______ below the safety limits.
questions.explain: Đoạn F: xét nghiệm mật ong của nhiều thành phố cho thấy "levels of heavy metals below the safety limits".

blocks.instructions: Look at the following statements and the list of locations below. Match each statement with the correct location, A–E. You may use any letter more than once.
options: A  Rooftops
B  Railway embankments
C  School grounds
D  Cemeteries
E  Private balconies

questions.q: Hives here are protected from theft but may suffer in bad weather.
questions.explain: Đoạn E: mái nhà an toàn khỏi trộm và kẻ phá hoại, nhưng tổ ong chịu "strong wind and summer heat".

questions.q: Bees can follow lines of wild flowers for long distances here.
questions.explain: Đoạn E: bờ đường ray ít người lui tới tạo thành "long corridors of wild flowers that bees can follow for kilometres".

questions.q: The hives help to teach young people about the natural world.
questions.explain: Đoạn E: ở sân trường, trẻ em kiểm tra tổ ong và học về côn trùng, thực phẩm, các mùa.

questions.q: The peace and quiet of the site is combined with a varied range of plants.
questions.explain: Đoạn E: nghĩa trang "combine silence with a rich mixture of flowering trees, shrubs and uncut grass".

questions.q: Keeping hives here is likely to upset the people living next door.
questions.explain: Đoạn E: ban công riêng thường không được khuyến khích vì dễ bị hàng xóm phàn nàn ("likely to lead to complaints").
